The Peru site has the lowest elevation at 3242.9 m and the lowest cold_dry value of 0.0138, but its airport is 195.7 km away.
The Pakistan site is an extreme case: highest elevation at 4589.1 m, farthest airport at 277.9 km, and highest cold_dry at 0.4483.
The Mars site has no context data, so its accessibility cannot be assessed and it is excluded from the ranking.

report.summary: Peru, India and Pakistan best match the Shackleton rim's terrain shape; all similarities are modest, mainly curvature and slope-direction differences.

claims.text: Peru has the highest terrain similarity of the three candidates, though the match is still modest.
Peru's main weakness is surface curvature, with a much larger convex share of its ground than the target.
India matches the target's local relief closely but diverges at the 36 km landform scale.
Pakistan has the lowest terrain match of the three, weakest in slope-direction variety and curvature.

report.summary: India's window ranks first on score and fits light within range; surface fit is weak everywhere, and low-sun conditions cannot be reproduced on Earth.

claims.text: India's window ranks first and matches the Moon's sun regime with light_sim 0.8329, inside the Earth range of 0.7389 to 0.9527.
Peru's and Pakistan's windows also fall inside that range, at light_sim 0.7806 and 0.8449.
The Moon's median sun elevation is near the horizon, while India and Peru sit well above it, so low-sun conditions cannot be reproduced.
Terrain fit is weak at every candidate, and the light model is analytic, so local shadowing is not captured.

report.summary: Four field tests for Shackleton rim: India for low-sun navigation, Peru for slope traverse, Pakistan for shadowed operations, Peru for comms relay.

claims.text: Low-sun navigation drill at the India site, matching the target's low light profile during its December to January window.
Slope traverse on the Peru ground, where mean slope and local relief are closest to the Shackleton rim.
Shadowed-area operations at the Pakistan highland, the coldest and driest twin, to rehearse permanently shadowed ground.
Comms relay drill at the Peru twin, scheduled in its June window, rehearsing low Earth elevation seen at landing.

limitations: Sunlight uses an analytic model: circular orbit, no eccentricity, no local horizon or terrain shadowing.
Similarity is terrain shape only (slope, roughness, relief, curvature); not geology, chemistry or regolith.
Terrain is compared at one common ground scale; features smaller than the grid spacing are not seen.
Environment data (country, climate, airport) is a coarse proxy for logistics; no routing or permits checked.
Terrain similarity is modest at every candidate site.
The light model is analytic and does not capture local shadowing.
